claims.text:
TITLE: Retrying a Failed Tool Call: Duplicate Side Effects and the Token Bill Nobody Meters
DESCRIPTION: A 650-trial local fault injection separates a stall before the commit from a stall after it. Regenerating the call id duplicated the effect in 50 of 50 post-commit trials, reusing it duplicated none, and the retry resent 5,640 characters where one call sent 1,920.

claims.note: Opening states the experiment size (650 trials, SQLite effect ledger) and links the retry-budget sibling post for the cost half; the duplicate count is a ledger read, not a log inference.

run.methodology: Same run as ledger.csv; summary.json is the aggregation the harness prints at the end (mean attempts and mean characters resent per cell). Re-running the harness reproduces both files from the same seed-free deterministic loop.

claims.text: The correct answer is not "retry less". It is that a retry is only safe when the server can recognise the second attempt as the same operation. This post measures the difference between the two failure shapes that a client cannot distinguish, and then measures what the retry costs in resent prompt text. The experiment is 650 trials on one host against a local tool server with a SQLite effect ledger, so the duplicate count is read from the database rather than inferred from logs. The retry budget half of this problem is covered in [the circuit-breaker and retry-budget guide](https://baeseokjae.github.io/posts/agent-cost-circuit-breaker-pattern-guide-2026/); this post is about the correctness half that assumes away.

claims.note: Quotes the draft's restatement of RFC 9110 method idempotency verbatim; the excerpt is in research/evidence/.../ietf-idempotency-key-draft-08.md.
claims.text: HTTP does not rescue you either, because agent tool calls are almost always writes. Per RFC 9110 as restated in the Idempotency-Key Internet-Draft, "the methods `OPTIONS`, `HEAD`, `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent while methods `POST` and `PATCH` are not" (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header). A tool call that creates a comment or a ticket is a POST. It inherits no idempotency guarantee from the protocol, so the guarantee has to be constructed by the caller and honoured by the server.

Stripe's API documentation shows what that construction looks like when it is done properly: the API "supports idempotency for safely retrying requests without accidentally performing the same operation twice", and for API v1 "Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a given idempotency key after endpoint execution begins. Retries with the same key return the saved response" (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests). That construction comes with an expiry, and the wording matters: "For API v1, you can remove keys from the system automatically after they're at least 24 hours old. We generate a new request if a key is reused after the original is pruned." That is permission for the operator to prune keys, not a promise that Stripe expires them on a timer, and it still fixes the boundary a retry loop lives inside: once the key is gone, the same call id is a brand-new request.
claims.note: Three verbatim excerpts from the Stripe idempotent-requests page, checked against the saved render in the evidence directory: 'supports idempotency for safely retrying requests without accidentally performing the same operation twice'; 'Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a given idempotency key after endpoint execution begins. Retries with the same key return the saved response'; and the full two-sentence retention passage 'For API v1, you can remove keys from the system automatically after they're at least 24 hours old. We generate a new request if a key is reused after the original is pruned.' The r1 correction quotes that last passage as written instead of reflowing it into the passive, and the paragraph now states what it does not claim: it is operator permission to prune, not automatic vendor expiry.
Describes only this fixture's own construction (endpoint, effect table, stored responses) so the duplicate definition is checkable against the harness source.
claims.text: The experiment is deliberately small and offline: a `ThreadingHTTPServer` on 127.0.0.1 with one `POST /tool` endpoint, an append-only `effects` table in SQLite, and a `responses` table that stores the status and body under the request's `Idempotency-Key`. A duplicate is a second row in `effects` for the same trial, counted in the database after the client has finished, not inferred from the client's own bookkeeping.

claims.text: Three fault modes are injected at the server, and the client's timeout is 0.12 s while the late reply takes 0.35 s:

claims.note: Fault-mode table mirrors the four branches in Handler.do_POST of the published harness: none, error_502_before, timeout_before, timeout_after (first attempt only).
claims.text:
| Fault mode | What the server does | What the client sees |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | Commits, replies 200 | 200 |
| `error_502_before` | Replies 502 without touching the ledger | 502 |
| `timeout_before` | Sleeps past the client timeout, never commits | Timeout, every attempt |
| `timeout_after` | Commits first, then sleeps past the client timeout on the first attempt | Timeout on attempt 1, indistinguishable from `timeout_before` |

claims.note: Policy definitions mirror run_scenario in the published harness; the distinction under test is whether the original tool call id survives the retry.
claims.text: Four client policies run against those faults, and the difference between the first two is the whole subject of this post. Policy A retries up to three times, regenerating both the tool call id and the `Idempotency-Key` on each attempt. Policy B retries with the original tool call id reused as the `Idempotency-Key`. Policy C keeps regenerating keys but the server dedupes on `(tool, sha256(args))`. Policy D fails closed and never retries.

claims.text: Fifty trials run per policy per fault mode (four policies × three fault modes × 50 = 600), plus a 50-trial no-fault control under the blind policy, for 650 ledger rows in total. Two controls had to come out clean before any cell could be read as a finding: the no-fault cell had to commit exactly one effect per trial, and the pre-commit stall had to produce zero duplicates under every policy. The full matrix ran in 108.48 s of wall time on this host, with no model calls and no external network.

claims.text:
| Policy | Stall before commit | Stall after commit | 502 before commit |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: blind retry, new call id | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 4.0 attempts | **50/50 duplicates, 2 effects**, 2.0 attempts | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 4.0 attempts |
| B: retry, reuse call id | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 4.0 attempts | 0/50 duplicates, 1 effect, 2.0 attempts | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 4.0 attempts |
| C: arg-hash dedupe | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 4.0 attempts | 0/50 duplicates, 1 effect, 2.0 attempts | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 4.0 attempts |
| D: no retry | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 1.0 attempt | 0/50 duplicates, 1 effect, 1.0 attempt | 0/50 duplicates, 0 effects, 1.0 attempt |

The obvious objection is that duplicating after an injected post-commit stall is true by construction. It is, for policy A, and that is exactly why it is presented as a control rather than a discovery: it proves the injector commits before the client gives up, and that the ledger can see the second row. The finding is in the columns beside it. Under the same injected fault, reusing the original call id (B) and server-side argument-hash dedupe (C) both dropped to zero duplicates and left exactly one row in the ledger, by two different mechanisms: B's retry carried the same key and was answered from the response stored under it, while C's retry arrived with a fresh key and was caught by the argument-hash branch, which replied 200 with the id of the effect already written instead of inserting a second one. The pre-commit column is where matching outcomes hide different behaviour. All four policies wrote nothing and duplicated nothing there, but A, B and C averaged 4.0 attempts each against 1.0 for D, and every retrying client still finished with status 0 and no knowledge of whether anything had happened.
claims.note: Interprets the post-commit column against the pre-commit column, with every figure re-read from ledger.csv in this run (650 rows, 13 cells of 50). Post-commit: A 50/50 duplicate trials with 2 effects committed and mean 2.0 attempts; B and C 0/50 with 1 effect each and mean 2.0 attempts; D 0/50 with 1 effect and mean 1.0 attempt. The two mechanisms are distinguished from the harness source, not inferred: b_reuse_key resends the first call id as the Idempotency-Key and hits the responses table lookup in Store.commit, while c_arg_hash_dedupe mints a fresh idem_ key and is caught by the dedupe (tool, args_hash) branch, which returns status 200 with the original effect_id and stores that answer under the retry's new key. The r1 correction removes the earlier claim that all four policies behaved identically in the pre-commit column: duplicates and effects are zero for all four, but mean attempts are 4.0 for A, B and C against 1.0 for D, and final_status is 0 for all four.

claims.text: That last point is the part that gets lost in retry-policy debates. "Zero duplicates" is not the same as "safe". The pre-commit stall is the honest control for the opposite reason: no effect landed at all, and the retrying policies burned four attempts trying to establish an outcome they never got, ending with status 0 and an unknown result. Duplicate-freedom in that column is not a property of the policy; it is a property of the server never having written anything.

A 502 that never resolves is a fault no retry can fix, and the retrying policies spent four attempts and 13,080 characters per trial to establish that nothing was written. None of those attempts duplicated anything, because the server rejected them before the ledger, but none of them made progress either.

claims.note: Arithmetic on measured means: 5,640/1,920 = 2.94 and 13,080/1,920 = 6.81. The block explicitly declines to convert characters into tokens or a price.
claims.text: The 2.94× is the number a step meter hides. The meter records one tool step; the executions were two; the prompt text sent is 2.94 times what a single execution sends at this payload size. The 6.81× is what a retry loop costs when the fault never clears — and in the 502 column it bought nothing at all. These are character counts from this fixture, not billed tokens: no tokenizer and no vendor price was applied, so the ratios describe the shape of the multiplication, not a dollar figure. The mechanism that makes step meters under-count is the same one described in [the guide to token meters for agent cost tracking](https://baeseokjae.github.io/posts/token-usage-meters-for-agent-cost-tracking/), which counts a logical step per recorded call.

claims.text: There is a second, quieter cost in the blind-retry policy: the regenerated call id is what made the duplicate possible. In the post-commit column, the call id changed on 50 of 50 policy-A trials and on 0 of 50 under policies B and C, and that difference is the mechanism, not a side effect. A retry wrapper that rebuilds the request from scratch — new id, new key, same arguments — is a duplicate generator the moment the first attempt committed. A retry wrapper that carries the original id forward is a dedupe client.

claims.note: Recommendation grounded in the measured contrast (50/50 to 0/50 when the call id is carried into the key); the change is described as tested only in this fixture.

run.methodology: Same run as ledger.csv; summary.json is the aggregation the harness prints at the end (mean attempts and mean characters resent per cell). Re-running the harness reproduces both files from the same seed-free deterministic loop.

claims.text: Carry the tool call id into the idempotency key and do not mint a new one on retry. That single change took the post-commit column from 50/50 to 0/50 here, and it costs nothing in the happy path because the key is only consulted when a retry arrives. If your wrapper builds a fresh request object per attempt, the call id is usually sitting in the original request and only has to be threaded through the retry path rather than regenerated.

Treat the retention window as a real boundary. A stored response only prevents a duplicate while it is still stored; Stripe documents 24 hours as the earliest age at which an API v1 key can be removed, and a key reused after the original is pruned generates a new request. Any retry, replay, or queue-drain path that can run later than the window needs a durable causation record of its own.
claims.note: Restates the Stripe retention wording as documented, without upgrading it into a vendor guarantee: the page says 'For API v1, you can remove keys from the system automatically after they're at least 24 hours old. We generate a new request if a key is reused after the original is pruned.' 'Earliest age at which a key can be removed' is what that sentence supports; the durable-causation recommendation that follows is the author's guidance, not a Stripe claim.
Limitations of this fixture: single host, loopback, deterministic timings, first-attempt-only stall, four-attempt cap, identical-argument retries. No vendor behaviour is characterised.
claims.text: This is one HTTP server, one SQLite file and a loopback network on a single host. No vendor endpoint, load balancer, or multi-region retry path was exercised, and no named product's retry behaviour is being characterised. The 0.12 s client timeout against a 0.35 s reply is chosen to make the race deterministic, not to model production latency. Only the first attempt of a post-commit trial stalls; a fault that stalls every attempt was run in an earlier pass and discarded because no retry could ever observe the stored response. Retries stop at four attempts, so nothing here says what happens across a process restart, and the argument-hash policy only covers retries that send identical arguments.
